title: Numbers, age, and addresses
goal: Count from zero to the millions, give your age, phone number, and address — while enjoying one rule that is simpler than English: after a number, the noun stays singular.
bekal: build any number up to a thousand without memorizing each one
answer *Hány éves vagy?* and ask it back
use ordinal numbers for floors, dates, and order

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Az iskola irodájában
dialogs.intro: Budi is enrolling at the language school's office. The secretary fills in a form as she asks questions.

notes: **Két or kettő, once more.** *Kettő* is used when the number stands alone — answering a question, reading a phone number, giving a house number. *Két* is used when a noun follows: *két tanár*, *két hét*. Look at the dialogue: Budi answers *Tizenkettő?* (standing alone) after the secretary says *tizenkét diák* (with a noun).

**After a number, the noun stays singular — and so does the verb.** *Tizenkét diák **van***, not *vannak*. Unlike English ("there are twelve students"), Hungarian never pluralizes after a number, so don't let English habits creep in.

**Hány for countable things, mennyi for amounts.** *Hány diák?* (how many students), *Mennyi idő?* (how much time), *Mennyi pénz?* (how much money). Choosing wrong isn't fatal, but *hány* before an uncountable noun sounds odd right away — just like "how many water" in English.

**Hét does double duty.** It means "seven" **and** "week". The sentence tells them apart: *hét diák* (seven students) versus *nyolc hét* (eight weeks). This coincidence will never truly confuse you, but it always makes beginners smile the first time they notice it.

**Numbers are written as one word, with no "and".** *huszonnégy* (twenty-four), *harminchét* (thirty-seven), *százhúsz* (one hundred twenty). Hungarian joins them into a single word up to two thousand. Above that, hyphens appear.

grammars.title: Zero to twenty-nine
body: Learn the first eleven numbers by heart; the rest is just assembly.
after: Teens are built from **tizen-** + the unit, and the twenties from **huszon-** + the unit. Notice that *tíz* shortens to *tizen-* and *húsz* changes to *huszon-* — these two changes are the only things to memorize in the whole number system.
From thirty on, the pattern is straight with no surprises: the tens are written in full and the unit is attached.

grammars.title: Tens, hundreds, thousands
body: After twenty, Hungarian stops being difficult.
after: Hundreds and thousands use *két-*, not *kettő-*: *kétszáz* (200), *kétezer* (2,000). Once again the same rule — something follows, so the form is *két*.

For years, Hungarians read them out as one full number: *ezerkilencszázkilencvennyolc* (1998), *kétezer-huszonhat* (2026). Long, but no shortcut — and one of the best pronunciation workouts you can get.

grammars.title: Ordinal numbers
body: Used for floors, dates, order, and the unit numbers in this course.
after: The ending is *-dik*, with a linking vowel following vowel harmony. Two rebels: *első* and *második* — and they are the most frequently used, so memorize them outright.
In writing, ordinals are marked by a **period** after the digit: *2. emelet* is read *második emelet*. That period is not a full stop; it is part of the number.

head: Magyar
Say it
English
rows: How many of you are there?

blocks.text: *Hányan vagytok?* uses a special form for counting people: *ketten* (two of us/them), *hárman* (three), *négyen* (four), *öten* (five). English has no equivalent beyond phrases like "the two of us", but the Hungarian forms are short and tidy.
Hungarian addresses are written from the biggest unit to the smallest, and each part has its own word that cannot be swapped.

Written out in full, Budi's address becomes: **1074 Budapest, Rákóczi út 27. 2. em. 6.** A Budapest postal code is always four digits starting with 1, and the middle two digits give the district — 1074 means district seven. Every Hungarian uses this little trick to guess where an address is.

blocks.title: Two phrases you must know when filling in forms
items: *Hogy írjuk?* — "How do we write it?" Used to ask for a spelling, and very handy because your name will almost certainly be misspelled.
*Betűzném.* — "Let me spell it." Then say it letter by letter. Names with *y* and *u* side by side almost always need this treatment.
